content:
Arthritis is a common condition that causes pain and inflammation in joints. It is not one disease but a group of many different conditions. The most common in the UK are osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. Arthritis can affect people of any age, including children. There is usually no cure, but treatment can reduce pain, keep you moving and, for inflammatory types, prevent damage.

How common is it?

Arthritis and related musculoskeletal conditions affect millions of people in the UK. It is one of the most common reasons for visiting a GP and for time off work. Osteoarthritis is the most common type, followed by rheumatoid arthritis.

How a joint works

A joint is where two bones meet. The ends of the bones are covered with smooth cartilage, and the joint is surrounded by a capsule lined with tissue that produces lubricating fluid. Muscles, tendons and ligaments support and move the joint. Arthritis can affect any part of this system.

Common symptoms

  • joint pain, tenderness and stiffness
  • swelling and warmth
  • restricted movement
  • weakness and muscle wasting
  • tiredness, particularly in inflammatory arthritis

Main types

  • Osteoarthritis: the joint lining wears and the joint struggles to repair. It mainly affects knees, hips, hands and spine.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis: the immune system attacks the joints, often the hands and feet on both sides.
  • Psoriatic arthritis: linked with psoriasis.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis: mainly affects the spine.
  • Gout: crystals form in a joint, causing sudden severe pain.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: affects children and young people.

How arthritis is diagnosed

Your GP will ask about your symptoms and examine your joints. NICE (NG226) says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed without tests in people over 45 with typical symptoms. If inflammatory arthritis is suspected, you may have blood tests and should be referred to a rheumatologist. X-rays, ultrasound or MRI may be used in some cases.

Treatment

Treatment depends on the type of arthritis.

  • Exercise is a core treatment for all types. It reduces pain and stiffness and builds strength.
  • Weight management reduces strain on hips and knees.
  • Pain relief, including topical anti-inflammatory gels and painkillers. Ask your pharmacist what suits you.
  • Physiotherapy and occupational therapy for exercise, aids and joint protection.
  • Disease-modifying medicines (DMARDs) and biologics for inflammatory arthritis.
  • Surgery, such as joint replacement, when other treatments have not helped.

Living with arthritis

  • keep active with a mix of aerobic, strengthening and stretching exercise
  • pace yourself to manage energy
  • use aids and gadgets to make tasks easier
  • look after your mood and sleep
  • know your rights at work under the Equality Act 2010
  • check which benefits you may be entitled to

Support in the UK

Your GP is your first point of contact. Many areas also offer self-referral to physiotherapy. Charities, including Living With Arthritis, provide information and support. Your council can assess your needs at home for equipment and adaptations.

When to see a GP

See your GP if you have joint pain, swelling or stiffness that lasts more than a few weeks, or if pain is stopping you from doing everyday things. Seek help sooner if you have several swollen joints or stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes in the morning.

Outlook

Arthritis affects everyone differently. Many people find their symptoms are manageable with the right mix of treatment, activity and support, and continue to work and enjoy their usual activities.

Questions to ask at your first appointment

  • What type of arthritis do I have?
  • What can I do myself to help?
  • Would physiotherapy or other support help me?
  • What should I do if it gets worse?

Understanding your type of arthritis is the first step towards managing it well.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
